title: All three SkyLink bridges share one security template, trading independent review for correlated risk
content:
The Solana (A.4.2.2.2), Avalanche (A.4.2.2.3) and Plasma (A.4.2.2.4) sections are structurally identical: same Token/Governance split, same dual-sided freezer arrangement, word-for-word identical Usage Standards, same net accounting definition, same 2/2 and 4/7 validator quorums, same 2-of-N freezer thresholds. The only genuine variation is which organizations hold freezer seats and what the numeric rate limits are.

That uniformity is a deliberate asset. Adding a chain becomes an instantiation rather than a design exercise; reviewers, responders and integrators learn one model and apply it everywhere; and the Atlas can state a security property once and have it hold across the fleet. It also makes the shared Ethereum freezer coherent, since a single switch over heterogeneous bridges would be far harder to reason about.

The cost is correlation. Each deployment is not an independent bet: a defect in the template — in the net-accounting logic, in the 2/2 assumption, in the LayerZero dependency common to every validator set — is present on every chain at once. The bridges are diversified across ecosystems but not across designs.

The Atlas partially acknowledges this with the fleet-wide Ethereum freezer, which is exactly the tool a correlated failure needs. What it does not do is vary the design between chains to reduce the correlation, which is a defensible choice — heterogeneous bridges would multiply the number of distinct things that can be wrong — but one worth stating explicitly when assessing SkyLink's aggregate risk.
description: Solana, Avalanche and Plasma repeat the same freezer design, usage standards, net accounting and validator quorums verbatim, so a flaw in the template is a flaw in every deployment.
